concepts.title: 1. Modal Class and Mode Formula
concepts.subtitle: Locate the peak and estimate the mode
concepts.summary: The modal class is the class interval with the highest frequency. The grouped-data mode is estimated using the lower boundary of the modal class and the frequencies of the modal, preceding, and succeeding classes.

points.text: Choose the interval with the greatest frequency $f_1$.

concepts.trap: Using the modal frequency itself as the mode.

concepts.title: 2. Missing Frequency from Given Mode
concepts.subtitle: Turn the mode formula into an equation
concepts.summary: When one frequency is missing and the mode is known, place the unknown frequency in the correct modal or adjacent-frequency position, substitute the known mode, and solve the resulting equation.

points.text: Keep the unknown as $f$ in the relevant frequency position.
Cross-multiply the mode equation to solve for $f$.

concepts.trap: Treating the missing frequency as a class mark or ignoring its location.

concepts.title: 3. Mean–Mode Comparison
concepts.subtitle: Interpret two measures together
concepts.summary: In contextual grouped data, calculate the mean from class marks and the mode from the modal class, then compare the two statistics numerically.

points.text: Compute the grouped mode and compare the two values.

concepts.trap: Comparing modal frequency with the mean instead of comparing mean and mode.

concepts.title: 4. Continuous and Discontinuous Classes
concepts.subtitle: Adjust boundaries before using the formula
concepts.summary: For discontinuous integer class intervals, convert boundaries by subtracting 0.5 from lower limits and adding 0.5 to upper limits, then apply the mode formula with the adjusted lower boundary.

points.text: Use the adjusted lower boundary in the mode formula.

concepts.trap: Applying the continuous-class mode formula to unadjusted discontinuous limits.
